title: Acids, Bases and Salts
summary: Every day we meet sour acids and bitter bases. This chapter trains you to identify them using indicators like litmus, turmeric, china rose, phenolphthalein, methyl orange and even olfactory indicators such as onion. It then works through the chemical properties: acids with metals, metal carbonates and metal hydrogencarbonates releasing hydrogen and carbon dioxide, and the mutual neutralisation of acids and bases to form salt and water. The common feature of all acids is the production of H3O+ ions, and of all bases the production of OH- ions, and both need water to show their behaviour. The pH scale is then connected with daily life, from tooth decay below pH 5.5 to digestion, plant growth and stings. Finally, the chapter surveys salts, their families and the nature of their solutions, and the four industrially important chemicals from common salt: sodium hydroxide, bleaching powder, baking soda and washing soda, closing with plaster of Paris and water of crystallisation.

Reaction of acids with metals and the pop sound test
Reaction with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates and the limewater test
H3O+ and OH- ions and the need of water for acidity
Strong and weak acids and bases
pH scale and importance of pH in daily life
Family of salts and pH of salt solutions

Water of crystallisation and plaster of Paris

sections.heading: Indicators: Telling Acids from Bases
sections.para: We must never taste laboratory chemicals, so we use indicators, substances that show one colour in acidic solutions and another in basic solutions. Litmus, a purple dye extracted from lichens, turns red in acids and blue in bases; neutral litmus paper is purple. Turmeric stain turns reddish brown with soap, a base. Phenolphthalein stays colourless in acids but becomes pink in bases. Methyl orange is red in acids and yellow in bases. Extracts of coloured flowers, like the magenta solution of china rose petals, turn deep pink in acids and green in bases. Olfactory indicators such as onion and vanilla lose their characteristic smell in bases, so the nose also works as an indicator. A single drop of the right indicator instantly reveals whether a solution is acidic, basic or neutral, which is why every acid-base experiment in the laboratory begins with adding a few drops of indicator.
points: Indicator: a substance that changes colour to show whether a solution is acidic or basic; litmus is obtained from lichens.
Litmus paper: blue litmus turns red in acids; red litmus turns blue in bases; in neutral solutions no change occurs.
Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic solutions and pink in basic solutions, making it ideal for titration of HCl with NaOH.
Methyl orange is red in acids and yellow in bases.
China rose indicator: acidic solutions turn deep pink or magenta while basic solutions turn green.
Turmeric is a natural indicator: its yellow stain turns reddish brown in bases like soap and back to yellow with acid.
Olfactory indicators like onion and vanilla essence lose their smell in bases, so smell change identifies a base.

keyTerms.meaning: A dye that shows different colours in acidic and basic solutions.
Purple natural dye from lichens; red in acids, blue in bases.
Synthetic indicator, colourless in acids and pink in bases.
Extract of Hibiscus petals; deep pink in acids and green in bases.
A substance whose smell changes in acidic or basic media, e.g. onion and vanilla.

sections.trick: BASE turns litmus BLUE (B-B pair) and phenolphthalein PINK (B-P pair); ACID does the opposite. China rose is the moody one: pink in acid, green in base.
sections.examPointer: Matching indicators with colours in acids and bases is a steady 1-2 mark MCQ area; china rose and turmeric colours have been asked as assertion-reason items.

sections.heading: Reaction of Acids with Metals
sections.para: When an acid reacts with a metal, hydrogen gas is evolved and a corresponding salt is formed, following the word pattern: acid plus metal gives salt plus hydrogen. Zinc granules dropped into dilute sulphuric acid bubble vigorously: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2. When the gas is passed through a soap solution, soap bubbles filled with hydrogen rise; if a burning candle is brought near a bubble, it burns with a pop sound, which is the confirmatory test for hydrogen. Magnesium reacts even faster with dilute hydrochloric acid, Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2, while copper shows no reaction with dilute acids because it is less reactive than hydrogen. Metals like zinc and aluminium also react with strong bases like sodium hydroxide to give hydrogen, e.g. Zn + 2NaOH -> Na2ZnO2 + H2, showing that the behaviour of metals with bases is not as simple as with acids.
points: General pattern: Acid + Metal -> Salt + Hydrogen gas.
Zinc with dilute sulphuric acid: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2; brisk effervescence of hydrogen is seen.
Test for hydrogen: pass the gas through soap solution and bring a burning candle to a bubble; the gas burns with a pop sound.
Magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2; the reaction is faster than with zinc.
Copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric or sulphuric acid because copper is below hydrogen in reactivity.
Some metals react with bases: Zn + 2NaOH -> Na2ZnO2 + H2, so hydrogen is also evolved when certain metals react with strong bases.

keyTerms.meaning: Reaction of a reactive metal with an acid producing a salt and hydrogen gas.
Confirmatory test for hydrogen: the gas burns with a pop sound near a flame.
Na2ZnO2, the salt formed when zinc reacts with sodium hydroxide.
Rapid bubbling of a gas out of a liquid during a reaction.

sections.trick: Acid meets metal, hydrogen flies: AM-SH. Remember the pop sound as hydrogen signing its autograph.
sections.examPointer: Writing the equation with hydrogen test (2 marks) and the exception question of why copper shows no reaction are repeatedly asked; metal plus base is a favourite MCQ.

sections.heading: Reactions with Metal Carbonates and Hydrogencarbonates
sections.para: All metal carbonates and hydrogencarbonates react with acids to give a corresponding salt, carbon dioxide gas and water. Marble chips or sodium carbonate dropped into dilute hydrochloric acid fizz briskly: Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2. Similarly sodium hydrogencarbonate gives NaHCO3 + HCl -> NaCl + H2O + CO2. When this carbon dioxide is passed through lime water, the solution turns milky because insoluble calcium carbonate is formed: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O. If carbon dioxide is passed in excess, the milkiness disappears as soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate forms, CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 -> Ca(HCO3)2. The limewater turning milky is the standard confirmatory test for carbon dioxide. The same chemistry makes cakes rise: baking powder releases CO2 on heating or with acid, and the soda-acid fire extinguisher sprays CO2 produced by sodium hydrogencarbonate reacting with sulphuric acid.
points: General pattern: Acid + Metal carbonate -> Salt + Water + Carbon dioxide.
Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2; brisk effervescence of CO2 is observed with marble chips too.
Acid + Metal hydrogencarbonate: NaHCO3 + HCl -> NaCl + H2O + CO2; reaction is faster than with the carbonate.
Test for CO2: pass the gas into lime water, Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O, and the lime water turns milky.
Excess CO2 dissolves the precipitate: CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 -> Ca(HCO3)2, so milkiness disappears on continued passage.
Baking powder contains baking soda and tartaric acid; on heating or mixing, CO2 makes cakes soft and fluffy, while tartaric acid neutralises the bitter taste of soda.
Soda-acid fire extinguisher: reaction of sodium hydrogencarbonate with sulphuric acid releases CO2, which surrounds the fire.

keyTerms.meaning: Salt of a metal with the carbonate ion CO3, e.g. Na2CO3 and CaCO3.
Salt containing the HCO3 ion, e.g. baking soda NaHCO3.
Confirmatory test for CO2 in which lime water turns milky due to CaCO3 formation.
Mixture of baking soda and a mild edible acid like tartaric acid used in baking.
Device generating CO2 from NaHCO3 and acid to extinguish fires.

sections.trick: Carbonate plus acid always ends in CO2: remember the trio salt-water-CO2. Lime water turns milky because CO2 converts clear Ca(OH)2 into cloudy CaCO3.
sections.examPointer: The limewater test with both equations, including disappearance of milkiness in excess CO2, is a repeated 2-3 marker; baking powder chemistry appears in case-based questions.

sections.heading: Neutralisation: Acids Meet Bases
sections.para: When an acid reacts with a base, the properties of both are destroyed and a salt with water is formed; this is neutralisation. Hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide gives sodium chloride and water: NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O. In terms of ions, the acid supplies H+ (existing as hydronium, H3O+) and the base supplies OH-, and these combine to form water: H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l), while the remaining ions make the salt. Neutralisation is exothermic, and the solution becomes neutral only when the amounts are exactly balanced. The reaction has wide use: antacid tablets and milk of magnesia neutralise excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach, farmers add slaked lime or quicklime to acidic soil, and factories neutralise acidic wastes with basic solutions before disposal. A drop of phenolphthalein makes the endpoint visible, as the pink colour of the base disappears when exactly neutralised.
points: Neutralisation: Acid + Base -> Salt + Water; both acidic and basic characters are destroyed.
NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O; common salt is the product of neutralising caustic soda with hydrochloric acid.
Ionic view: H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l); the H+ exists as hydronium ion H3O+ in water.
Neutralisation reactions are generally exothermic and release heat.
Indigestion is treated with antacids like milk of magnesia, a mild base that neutralises excess stomach acid.
Farmers treat acidic soil with slaked lime or quicklime to restore a pH suitable for crops.
With phenolphthalein, the pink NaOH solution turns colourless the moment exact neutralisation by acid is reached.

keyTerms.meaning: Reaction between an acid and a base forming salt and water, destroying both characters.
Ionic compound formed by replacing the hydrogen of an acid by a metal or similar ion.
A mild base like magnesium hydroxide taken to neutralise excess stomach acid.
Neutralisation releases heat, warming the reaction mixture.

sections.trick: Acid plus base ends in a handshake: H+ and OH- join to make water, the leftovers hold hands as salt. Every antidote is just a neutralisation: antacid for acid, lime for sour soil.
sections.examPointer: Neutralisation equations and daily-life applications (antacid, soil treatment) are regular 2-3 markers; the ionic equation H+ + OH- -> H2O is asked for one mark.

sections.heading: What Do All Acids and All Bases Have in Common
sections.para: All acids generate hydrogen ions, H+, only in the presence of water, and all bases generate hydroxide ions, OH-, when dissolved in water. Hydrogen ions cannot exist naked in solution; they combine with a water molecule to form the hydronium ion: HCl + H2O -> H3O+ + Cl-. Similarly solid NaOH releases Na+ and OH- ions in water. This explains why dry hydrogen chloride gas does not turn dry litmus red, because there is no water to form H3O+ ions, while aqueous hydrochloric acid turns litmus red immediately. It also explains why glucose and alcohol, though containing hydrogen, are not acids: they do not ionise to give H+ in solution. Acids like HCl that ionise almost completely in water are strong acids; acetic acid, which ionises only partially, is a weak acid. Similarly NaOH and KOH are strong bases, while ammonium hydroxide is a weak base.
points: Acids produce H+ ions in water, and H+ exists as the hydronium ion: HCl + H2O -> H3O+ + Cl-.
Bases produce OH- ions in water: NaOH(s) -> Na+(aq) + OH-(aq); bases that dissolve in water are called alkalis.
Dry HCl gas does not affect dry litmus because without water no H3O+ ions can form; aqueous HCl turns blue litmus red.
Glucose and alcohol solutions do not conduct like acids because they contain no ions, showing that H+ ion, not hydrogen atoms, causes acidity.
Strong acids like HCl, H2SO4 and HNO3 ionise completely; weak acids like CH3COOH ionise only partially.
Strong bases like NaOH and KOH ionise completely in water; ammonium hydroxide is a weak base.
The strength of an acid or base is about degree of ionisation, while concentration is about amount dissolved; the two are different ideas.

keyTerms.meaning: H3O+, the form in which a hydrogen ion exists in aqueous solution.
A base that is soluble in water, e.g. NaOH and KOH.
An acid that ionises almost completely in water, e.g. HCl.
An acid that ionises only partially in water, e.g. acetic acid.
Separation of a compound into ions when dissolved in water.

sections.trick: No water, no acidity: H+ always needs a watery coat and becomes H3O+. Strong means fully broken into ions, weak means half-hearted ionisation.
sections.examPointer: Why dry HCl gas fails to turn dry litmus red, and why glucose is not an acid, are standard 2-mark questions; strong vs weak classification is common in MCQs.

sections.heading: The pH Scale: Measuring Acidity Precisely
sections.para: Colour indicators tell us whether a solution is acidic or basic, but to know how acidic or basic it is we use the pH scale, running from 0 to 14. pH means the power of hydrogen: it measures the concentration of H+ ions, but inversely, so the lower the pH, the greater the acidity. A neutral solution like pure water has pH 7. Solutions of pH less than 7 are acidic, and the smaller the number, the more acidic; solutions of pH more than 7 are basic, and the larger the number, the more basic. pH is measured with universal indicator paper, which shows a different colour for each pH value on the chart. This single number connects chemistry to daily life: blood is close to pH 7.4, lemon juice about 2.2, and a change of even one unit means a tenfold change in acidity, which is why small pH shifts matter so much to living things.
points: pH scale ranges from 0 to 14; pH 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 basic.
Lower pH means higher concentration of H+ ions, so stronger acidity; higher pH means stronger basicity.
A one-unit change in pH means a tenfold change in H+ concentration, so pH 2 is ten times more acidic than pH 3.
Universal indicator shows a whole range of colours matched against a chart to read the pH of a solution.
Reference values: gastric juice about 1.2, lemon juice 2.2, vinegar 3.0, tomato juice 4.1, blood 7.4, milk of magnesia 10.5, sodium hydroxide 14.
Strong acids have very low pH and strong bases have very high pH, while weak ones stay near the middle.

keyTerms.meaning: Scale from 0 to 14 measuring how acidic or basic a solution is.
pH 7, as in pure water, where H+ and OH- concentrations are equal.
A mixture of dyes giving different colours at different pH values.
Proportional to H+ ion concentration, shown inversely by the pH value.

sections.trick: pH is a reverse ruler: smaller number, stronger acid. Remember 7 in the middle like the zero of a number line, acid on the left, base on the right.
sections.examPointer: Reading and comparing pH values of given solutions and identifying the strongest acid or base is a frequent 2-3 mark question and a common case-based sub-part.

sections.heading: Importance of pH in Everyday Life
sections.para: Living systems work within narrow pH ranges, and the chapter lists four famous examples. First, tooth decay: bacteria in the mouth act on sugars and food particles to produce acids, and when the pH of the mouth falls below 5.5, the acid attacks tooth enamel, the hardest substance in the body; brushing with basic toothpaste after meals neutralises the acid and prevents decay. Second, indigestion: the stomach produces hydrochloric acid, and excess acid causes pain; antacids of pH around 10, like milk of magnesia, neutralise it. Third, soil pH: plants need a specific soil pH, and acidic soil is treated with quicklime or slaked lime to raise the pH. Fourth, self-defence by plants and animals: the stinging hair of nettle leaves injects methanoic acid, causing pain, and the traditional remedy is rubbing the leaf of the dock plant, which often grows beside the nettle and contains a base.
points: Tooth decay begins when mouth pH falls below 5.5; bacteria convert sugar into acid that corrodes enamel.
Brushing with basic toothpaste neutralises mouth acid and raises the pH above the danger level.
Excess HCl in the stomach causes indigestion; mild bases like milk of magnesia neutralise it safely.
Most crop plants need near-neutral soil; farmers add quicklime or slaked lime to reduce soil acidity.
Nettle leaf stinging hair injects methanoic acid; the juice of the dock plant, a natural base, relieves the pain.
The body maintains blood pH close to 7.4, and even small deviations can be dangerous, showing the sensitivity of life to pH.

keyTerms.meaning: Hardest substance in the body, corroded by mouth acids below pH 5.5.
Formic acid, injected by nettle stinging hairs causing burning pain.
Plant whose basic leaf juice neutralises nettle sting; often grows near nettles.
Adding bases like quicklime to acidic soil to adjust pH for healthy crops.

sections.trick: pH daily-life quartet: TEETH (5.5), TUMMY (antacid), SOIL (lime), STING (nettle and dock). Below 5.5, teeth take a dive.
sections.examPointer: Why toothpaste prevents decay and how the body deals with stings are classic give-reason questions of 2-3 marks; the pH 5.5 figure is a guaranteed MCQ.

sections.heading: Salts: Families and the pH of Salt Solutions
sections.para: A salt is an ionic compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal ion, and neutralisation leaves behind salts. Salts having the same positive or negative radicals are said to belong to the same family: NaCl and Na2SO4 belong to the sodium family sharing Na+, while NaCl and KCl share the chloride ion. The pH of a salt solution depends on the strength of the acid and base that formed it. A salt of a strong acid and a strong base, like NaCl, gives a neutral solution of pH 7. A salt of a strong acid and a weak base, like ammonium chloride formed from HCl and NH4OH, gives an acidic solution with pH less than 7. A salt of a weak acid and a strong base, like sodium carbonate or sodium acetate, gives a basic solution with pH greater than 7. Common salt is itself the raw material for many important chemicals studied in the next section.
points: Salt: ionic compound formed by neutralisation of an acid by a base, e.g. NaCl, CuSO4, Na2CO3.
Family of salts: salts sharing the same cation or anion, e.g. NaCl, Na2SO4 and Na2CO3 belong to the sodium family.
Strong acid + strong base salt like NaCl gives a neutral solution, pH 7.
Strong acid + weak base salt like NH4Cl gives an acidic solution, pH below 7.
Weak acid + strong base salts like Na2CO3 and CH3COONa give basic solutions, pH above 7.
Common salt, sodium chloride, is obtained by evaporation of sea water and is the starting material of the chlor-alkali industry.

keyTerms.meaning: Group of salts sharing the same positive or the same negative radical.
Salt of a strong acid and weak base whose solution has pH below 7, e.g. NH4Cl.
Salt of a weak acid and strong base whose solution has pH above 7, e.g. Na2CO3.
Salt of strong acid and strong base, e.g. NaCl, with solution pH 7.

sections.trick: The solution remembers its parents: strong parent dominates. Strong acid wins makes acidic NH4Cl; strong base wins makes basic Na2CO3; equal parents make neutral NaCl.
sections.examPointer: Predicting acidic, basic or neutral nature of given salt solutions is a regular 2-3 marker; NH4Cl and Na2CO3 are the two standard examples asked.

sections.heading: Chemicals from Common Salt: The Chlor-Alkali Family
sections.para: Common salt is not only a food ingredient but also the raw material for a family of industrially important chemicals. When electricity is passed through brine, an aqueous solution of sodium chloride, it decomposes: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2. Because the products are an alkali, NaOH, and chlorine, this is called the chlor-alkali process; chlorine is released at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide remains in the solution. Sodium hydroxide is used in making soaps and detergents and for degreasing metals; chlorine is used for water treatment, for making PVC, insecticides and bleaching powder; hydrogen is used as a fuel, in hydrogenation of oils and for making ammonia for fertilisers. Passing chlorine over dry slaked lime gives bleaching powder, Ca(OH)2 + Cl2 -> CaOCl2 + H2O, used for bleaching cotton, wood pulp and for disinfecting drinking water.
points: Chlor-alkali process: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2 when electricity passes through brine.
Chlorine is liberated at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode, while sodium hydroxide forms in the solution near the cathode.
Uses of NaOH: manufacture of soaps and detergents, paper making and degreasing of metals.
Uses of Cl2: water disinfection, swimming pools, manufacture of bleaching powder, PVC and insecticides.
Uses of H2: fuel, hydrogenation of vegetable oils to ghee, and production of ammonia for fertilisers.
Bleaching powder preparation: Ca(OH)2 + Cl2 -> CaOCl2 + H2O; chlorine acts on dry slaked lime.
Uses of bleaching powder: bleaching cotton and linen in textile industry, bleaching wood pulp in paper industry, and disinfecting drinking water.

keyTerms.meaning: Concentrated aqueous solution of sodium chloride used in the chlor-alkali process.
Electrolysis of brine giving NaOH, Cl2 and H2; named for the alkali and chlorine produced.
CaOCl2, made by the action of chlorine on dry slaked lime; used as bleaching and disinfecting agent.
Cl2 at anode and H2 at cathode during brine electrolysis.

sections.trick: Chlor-alkali gives three gifts: Cl2 at the anode (A-C pair), H2 at the cathode, and NaOH stays in the bath. Bleaching powder is born when chlorine meets dry slaked lime.
sections.examPointer: The chlor-alkali equation with products, electrodes and two uses of each is a favourite 5-marker; bleaching powder preparation equation is asked for 2 marks.

sections.heading: Baking Soda, Washing Soda and Their Uses
sections.para: Two more important chemicals come from the sodium family. Baking soda is sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO3, a mild non-corrosive base. On heating it decomposes: 2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2. It is used as an antacid for neutralising excess stomach acid, as an additive in baking powder along with tartaric acid, and in soda-acid fire extinguishers. The CO2 released in baking makes cakes and bread soft and spongy, while tartaric acid neutralises any bitter taste of sodium carbonate that may form. Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3.10H2O, obtained by recrystallising sodium carbonate from its solution. Its uses are wide: in the glass, soap and paper industries, in the manufacture of borax, for removing permanent hardness of water, and as a household cleaning agent for floors and drains. Both salts show how one raw material, common salt, branches into many everyday products through simple chemistry.
points: Baking soda is sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO3, a mild non-corrosive base.
On heating: 2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2; the released CO2 raises cakes and bread.
Uses of baking soda: antacid for acidity, ingredient of baking powder with tartaric acid, and in soda-acid fire extinguishers.
Tartaric acid in baking powder neutralises the bitter sodium carbonate formed on heating, so the cake does not taste bitter.
Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3.10H2O, prepared by recrystallisation of sodium carbonate solution.
Uses of washing soda: glass, soap and paper industries, manufacture of borax, removing permanent hardness of water, and as a cleaning agent.
Washing soda is also used to remove permanent hardness because carbonate precipitates out the calcium and magnesium ions of hard water.

keyTerms.meaning: Sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO3, a mild antacid and baking ingredient.
Sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3.10H2O, used in industries and for hard water.
Hardness of water due to dissolved chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium, removed by washing soda.
Dissolving and crystallising a salt again to obtain its hydrated pure form.

sections.trick: Baking soda is the gentle HCO3: antacid, cake-lifter, fire-fighter. Washing soda carries TEN waters (deca), so it washes glass, soap, paper and hard water all at once.
sections.examPointer: Preparation equations and two uses of each salt make a repeated 4-5 marker; why cakes become fluffy with the role of tartaric acid is a standing case-based sub-question.

sections.heading: Water of Crystallisation: Gypsum and Plaster of Paris
sections.para: Some salts fix a definite number of water molecules within their crystals as an essential part of their structure; this is called water of crystallisation. Blue vitriol, copper sulphate crystals, have the formula CuSO4.5H2O: on heating, the blue crystals turn white as they lose the five water molecules, and on adding water the white powder turns blue again, proving the water was built into the crystal. Gypsum, CaSO4.2H2O, contains two molecules of water per formula unit. On heating gypsum carefully at 373 K, it loses one and a half molecules of water to give plaster of Paris, CaSO4.1/2H2O, so named because huge deposits of gypsum were found near Paris. When plaster of Paris is mixed with water it sets into a hard solid mass of gypsum again in a short time, which is why it is used by doctors for supporting fractured bones, and by toy makers and decorators for smooth surfaces and statues.
points: Water of crystallisation: fixed number of water molecules present as part of a salt crystal, e.g. five in CuSO4.5H2O.
Heating blue copper sulphate: CuSO4.5H2O -> CuSO4 (white) + 5H2O; adding water turns it blue again, a reversible hydration.
Gypsum is calcium sulphate dihydrate, CaSO4.2H2O.
Plaster of Paris is prepared by heating gypsum at 373 K: CaSO4.2H2O -> CaSO4.1/2H2O + 3/2H2O.
The half water molecule is written because two CaSO4 units share one water molecule in the crystal.
On mixing with water, plaster of Paris sets to hard gypsum: CaSO4.1/2H2O + 3/2H2O -> CaSO4.2H2O.
Uses of plaster of Paris: supporting fractured bones, making toys, statues, decorative material and smooth surfaces; it must be stored in moisture-proof containers.

keyTerms.meaning: Fixed water molecules incorporated in the crystal structure of a salt.
Copper sulphate pentahydrate, CuSO4.5H2O, blue crystals that whiten on heating.
Calcium sulphate dihydrate, CaSO4.2H2O, the raw material of plaster of Paris.
Calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO4.1/2H2O, which sets into hard gypsum with water.

sections.trick: POP is gypsum minus one and a half waters: heat gypsum at 373 K to get POP, add water to get gypsum back. CuSO4.5H2O is blue with five, white with none.
sections.examPointer: POP preparation at 373 K with the equation, why it is stored in moisture-proof containers, and the blue-to-white copper sulphate experiment are repeated 2-5 mark questions.

mcqs.question: When a strip of blue litmus paper is dipped in a solution of sodium hydroxide, the colour
mcqs.explanation: NaOH is a base, and blue litmus stays blue in bases; only acids turn blue litmus red.

mcqs.question: While diluting concentrated sulphuric acid, the correct procedure is to
options: Add water to the acid quickly
Add the acid to water slowly with constant stirring
Heat the acid before adding water
mcqs.explanation: Dilution of a concentrated acid is highly exothermic; adding acid slowly to water with stirring spreads the heat safely, while water into acid can splash and cause burns.

mcqs.question: Dry hydrogen chloride gas does not turn dry blue litmus paper red because
options: There is no water to produce hydronium ions
Litmus needs a base to change colour
HCl gas is neutral in all conditions
mcqs.explanation: Acids show acidic behaviour only in water, where HCl forms H3O+ and Cl- ions; dry gas has no water, so no H3O+ is produced and litmus is unaffected.

mcqs.question: When zinc reacts with concentrated sodium hydroxide solution, the gas evolved is
mcqs.explanation: Zn + 2NaOH -> Na2ZnO2 + H2; amphoteric metals like zinc and aluminium evolve hydrogen with strong bases.

mcqs.question: When dilute hydrochloric acid is added to sodium carbonate, the gas evolved turns lime water
options: Colourless and odourless with no change
mcqs.explanation: Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2; carbon dioxide turns lime water milky due to formation of insoluble calcium carbonate.

mcqs.question: Milk of magnesia, used to cure indigestion, is
mcqs.explanation: Magnesium hydroxide is a mild base with pH about 10.5; it neutralises excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach.

mcqs.question: Which of the following compounds is used as an antacid?
mcqs.explanation: Baking soda, NaHCO3, is a mild non-corrosive base that neutralises excess stomach acid, so it is used in antacids.

mcqs.question: Tooth decay begins when the pH of the mouth falls below
mcqs.explanation: Below pH 5.5 the acid produced by mouth bacteria attacks tooth enamel; brushing with basic toothpaste raises the pH and protects the teeth.

mcqs.question: Among the following solutions, the one that is most strongly basic is the one with pH
mcqs.explanation: On the pH scale the larger the value above 7, the stronger the base; pH 14, like sodium hydroxide solution, is the most strongly basic.

mcqs.question: The aqueous solution of which of the following salts will be acidic?
mcqs.explanation: NH4Cl is a salt of a strong acid (HCl) and a weak base (NH4OH), so its solution is acidic; Na2CO3 and CH3COONa are basic and NaCl neutral.

mcqs.question: Bleaching powder is obtained by the reaction of chlorine with
mcqs.explanation: Ca(OH)2 + Cl2 -> CaOCl2 + H2O; chlorine acts on dry slaked lime to give bleaching powder, used for bleaching and disinfection.

mcqs.question: Plaster of Paris is prepared by heating gypsum at a temperature of
mcqs.explanation: At 373 K, CaSO4.2H2O loses one and a half molecules of water to form CaSO4.1/2H2O, plaster of Paris.

mcqs.question: On heating blue copper sulphate crystals, they turn white because
options: They lose their water of crystallisation
They react with oxygen to form copper oxide
mcqs.explanation: CuSO4.5H2O loses its five water molecules on heating and becomes white anhydrous CuSO4; it turns blue again on adding water.

mcqs.question: In the chlor-alkali process, the products formed at the cathode, in solution and at the anode respectively are
mcqs.explanation: In 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2, hydrogen is released at the cathode, sodium hydroxide forms in solution and chlorine at the anode.

mcqs.question: Baking powder makes cakes soft and spongy mainly because
options: Heating releases CO2 which makes the batter rise
mcqs.explanation: On heating or reacting with acid, NaHCO3 releases CO2, and the trapped gas makes the cake fluffy; tartaric acid only neutralises the bitter taste.

mcqs.question: China rose indicator when added to a basic solution turns it
mcqs.explanation: China rose extract is dark pink or magenta in acids but turns green in basic solutions.

mcqs.question: A few drops of phenolphthalein are added to NaOH solution and dilute HCl is added drop by drop. The colour change observed is
mcqs.explanation: Phenolphthalein is pink in the base; as HCl neutralises NaOH, the solution becomes acidic or neutral and the pink colour disappears.

mcqs.question: Washing soda, used for removing permanent hardness of water, has the formula
mcqs.explanation: Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3.10H2O; its carbonate ions precipitate Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions of hard water.

mcqs.question: The stinging hair of nettle leaves injects a liquid that causes burning pain. The substance injected and the traditional remedy are
options: Methanoic acid and juice of dock plant
mcqs.explanation: Nettle sting contains methanoic acid; the dock plant that usually grows nearby has basic juice which neutralises the acid and relieves the pain.

mcqs.question: An aqueous solution of glucose does not conduct electricity while hydrochloric acid solution does, because
options: Glucose is a covalent non-ionising compound while HCl ionises to give ions
mcqs.explanation: Conduction needs ions. HCl ionises in water to H3O+ and Cl-, but glucose dissolves as neutral molecules without forming ions, so it does not conduct.

boardQuestions.question: Why does dry hydrogen chloride gas not change the colour of dry litmus paper, whereas aqueous hydrochloric acid does?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Acids show their acidic behaviour only when they ionise in the presence of water to produce hydrogen ions, which exist as hydronium ions, H3O+. 2) Dry HCl gas contains only HCl molecules and no water, so no H3O+ ions are formed and the dry litmus paper remains unchanged. 3) In aqueous HCl, the gas dissolves and ionises as HCl + H2O -> H3O+ + Cl-, and the H3O+ ions turn blue litmus red. Thus water is essential for the acidic character of an acid to be observed.

boardQuestions.question: Write balanced chemical equations for the reaction of dilute hydrochloric acid with (a) zinc metal (b) sodium carbonate (c) sodium hydrogencarbonate. Name the gas evolved in each and state its test.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2; hydrogen gas is evolved, tested by bringing a burning candle near it, when it burns with a pop sound. 2) (b) Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2; carbon dioxide is evolved. 3) (c) NaHCO3 + HCl -> NaCl + H2O + CO2; carbon dioxide is evolved again. 4) Test for carbon dioxide: pass the gas through lime water, Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O, and the lime water turns milky; in excess CO2 the milkiness disappears as soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate forms. One mark for each balanced equation and the identification of the gas, plus the correct tests.

boardQuestions.question: Five solutions A, B, C, D and E have pH values 4, 1, 11, 7 and 9 respectively. (a) Which solution is neutral? (b) Which are strongly acidic and strongly basic? (c) Arrange the H+ concentration of A, B and C in increasing order.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) Solution D with pH 7 is neutral, since pH 7 corresponds to equal H+ and OH- concentrations as in pure water. 2) (b) Solution B with pH 1 is strongly acidic and solution C with pH 11 is strongly basic. 3) (c) A has pH 4, B has pH 1 and C has pH 11; since lower pH means higher H+ concentration, the increasing order of H+ concentration is C (pH 11) < A (pH 4) < B (pH 1). 4) Remember that pH is an inverse measure: a fall of one pH unit means a tenfold rise in acidity.

boardQuestions.question: What is the chlor-alkali process? Write the balanced equation, state where each product is obtained, and give two uses of each product.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) When electricity is passed through brine, an aqueous solution of sodium chloride, it decomposes to give sodium hydroxide, chlorine and hydrogen; since the products are an alkali and chlorine, the process is called the chlor-alkali process. 2) Equation: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2. Chlorine gas is liberated at the anode, hydrogen gas at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide is formed in the solution. 3) Uses of sodium hydroxide: manufacture of soaps and detergents, and degreasing of metals; it is also used in paper making. 4) Uses of chlorine: disinfecting drinking water and swimming pools, and manufacture of bleaching powder, PVC and insecticides. 5) Uses of hydrogen: as a clean fuel, for hydrogenation of vegetable oils into ghee, and for making ammonia which is used in fertilisers. Chlorine and hydrogen can also be combined to make hydrochloric acid used in medicines and cosmetics. The equation, electrode positions and uses carry the marks.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the preparation with balanced equations and give two uses each of bleaching powder, baking soda and washing soda.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Bleaching powder: chlorine gas acts on dry slaked lime, Ca(OH)2 + Cl2 -> CaOCl2 + H2O. It is used for bleaching cotton and linen in the textile industry and for disinfecting drinking water; it also bleaches wood pulp in the paper industry. 2) Baking soda: sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO3, is a mild non-corrosive base; on heating, 2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2. It is used as an antacid for acidity and as a component of baking powder along with tartaric acid, where the CO2 released makes cakes fluffy; it is also used in soda-acid fire extinguishers. 3) Washing soda: sodium carbonate solution is recrystallised to obtain sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3 + 10H2O -> Na2CO3.10H2O. It is used in the glass, soap and paper industries, for manufacture of borax, for removing permanent hardness of water, and as a household cleaning agent. All three chemicals come from the common salt family, showing its industrial importance.

boardQuestions.question: Read the source and answer: A white powder X is prepared by heating a mineral Y carefully at 373 K. When X is mixed with water, it sets into a hard solid mass, so doctors apply it to support fractured bones. (a) Identify X and Y with chemical formulae. (b) Write the equation for preparing X. (c) Why must X be stored in a moisture-proof container?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) X is plaster of Paris, calcium sulphate hemihydrate with formula CaSO4.1/2H2O, and Y is gypsum, calcium sulphate dihydrate with formula CaSO4.2H2O. 2) (b) On heating gypsum at 373 K: CaSO4.2H2O -> CaSO4.1/2H2O + 3/2H2O. The half water molecule is written because one water molecule is shared between two CaSO4 units in the crystal. 3) (c) Plaster of Paris absorbs moisture from the atmosphere and sets into a hard solid mass of gypsum, CaSO4.1/2H2O + 3/2H2O -> CaSO4.2H2O. Once set, it loses its smooth powdery form and becomes useless, so it must be kept in air-tight, moisture-proof containers. 4) When required, mixing with water gives a plastic paste that sets hard, which is why it supports fractured bones and is also used for making toys, statues, blackboard chalk and smooth decorative surfaces.

boardQuestions.question: Explain, with the help of pH, why toothpaste prevents tooth decay and why a basic toothpaste is advised after meals.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Bacteria present in the mouth act on sugar and food particles left after eating and produce acids. 2) The most critical factor is the pH of the mouth: when the pH falls below 5.5, the acid is strong enough to attack and corrode tooth enamel, the hardest substance in the body, starting tooth decay. 3) Toothpastes are generally basic, so brushing after meals neutralises the excess acid produced in the mouth and raises the pH above the danger value. 4) In this way, by maintaining the mouth pH above 5.5, toothpaste prevents the acid from attacking the enamel and protects the teeth from decay.

boardQuestions.question: Why should curd and sour food substances not be kept in containers made of brass or copper?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Curd and other sour substances like lemon juice and tamarind contain organic acids such as lactic acid and citric acid. 2) When kept in brass or copper vessels, these acids react chemically with the metal surface to form poisonous metallic compounds or salts. 3) Such vessels may also corrode, and the toxic products mix with the food, making it unfit and harmful for consumption. Hence sour foods are always stored in containers of glass, steel or food-grade material that do not react with acids.

boardQuestions.question: What happens when sodium hydrogencarbonate is heated during baking? Write the equation and explain the roles of CO2 and tartaric acid present in baking powder.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) On heating, baking soda decomposes: 2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2. 2) The carbon dioxide gas released gets trapped in the wet dough and expands on heating, raising the batter and making cakes and bread soft and spongy. 3) However, heating also produces sodium carbonate, which has a bitter taste. The tartaric acid mixed in baking powder reacts with sodium carbonate to neutralise it, removing the bitter taste, and any acid-base reaction additionally releases more CO2. 4) Thus CO2 gives the fluffiness and tartaric acid saves the taste, and together they make baking powder a complete leavening agent.

boardQuestions.question: Blue crystals of a salt are heated in a dry test tube; they turn white and drops of a liquid appear on the cooler walls. On adding a few drops of water to the white residue, the colour returns. Explain the observations and define the phenomenon involved.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) The blue crystals are copper sulphate pentahydrate, CuSO4.5H2O, which contains five molecules of water of crystallisation fixed in its crystal structure. 2) On heating, CuSO4.5H2O -> CuSO4 + 5H2O; the salt loses its water of crystallisation, the anhydrous copper sulphate formed is white, and the released water condenses as drops on the cooler walls of the tube. 3) On adding water, the anhydrous salt reabsorbs the water and turns blue again, CuSO4 + 5H2O -> CuSO4.5H2O. 4) The fixed number of water molecules chemically bound in the crystal of a salt is called its water of crystallisation; here it is five for copper sulphate.
